item.title: Alternating Current in the United States
item.description: Alternating Current in the United States Alternating current in the United States names the electrical system — transformers, polyphase generators and motors, and long-distance transmission — that won the contest with Edison-style direct current for heavy power distribution in the 1880s and 1890s.

item.title: Banking Reform and the Federal Reserve Act
item.description: Banking Reform and the Federal Reserve Act The Banking Reform and the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 established the modern central banking system of the United States, concluding a half-century struggle over the control of the national currency and credit.

item.title: Gospel of Wealth
item.description: Gospel of Wealth The Gospel of Wealth was the celebrated social philosophy articulated by steel industrialist andrew-carnegie in 1889 regarding the moral responsibilities of extreme wealth in a modern industrial democracy.

item.title: Gunpowder Trade Association
item.description: Gunpowder Trade Association The Gunpowder Trade Association, organized in April 1872 under Henry du Pont, was the pool through which American powder makers fixed the terms of an industry that e-i-du-pont-de-nemours-and-company came to dominate.

item.title: Highland Park Plant
item.description: Highland Park Plant The Highland Park plant in Michigan was the ford-motor-company factory, opened in 1910, where moving assembly and synchronized machine production brought the model-t to hundreds of thousands of units a year.

item.title: Mass Production in the United States
item.description: Mass Production in the United States Mass production in the United States is the industrial method — standardized parts, specialized machines, timed flow, and continuous output — that by 1919 had remade steel, electrical equipment, and above all the automobile.

item.title: Menlo Park Laboratory
item.description: Menlo Park Laboratory The Menlo Park laboratory in New Jersey was thomas-alva-edison’s “invention factory” of the late 1870s and early 1880s — a organized workshop of experimenters, machinists, and instruments that turned systematic trial into patented devices and newspaper spectacles.
